instruction: Do not open bleed or butcher any dead animal when anthrax is suspected.
Isolate live sick animals and keep people and other animals away from the area.
Mark and protect the site; avoid disturbing soil where animals graze or died.
Notify government veterinary services immediately for carcass disposal and diagnosis.
Vaccinate unaffected animals only under official veterinary direction after confirmation.
Isolate the affected animal immediately from the rest of the herd.
Stop all movement of animals vehicles and people off the farm until a veterinarian confirms the situation.
Provide soft palatable feed and clean water; avoid forcing the animal to walk on painful hooves.
Disinfect footwear tools and troughs that contacted saliva or blister fluid.
Notify the nearest government veterinary officer or livestock department without delay.
Isolate the animal to reduce insect exposure and limit spread within the herd.
Apply fly control measures on the farm (clean manure insecticide as advised locally).
Keep the animal in shade with fresh water and good-quality forage.
Do not burst or cut skin nodules; keep lesions clean and dry.
Contact a veterinarian for supportive care and official reporting if required in your district.
Strip out affected quarters gently and discard abnormal milk safely; do not feed it to calves.
Apply a clean cold compress to a hot swollen quarter for short periods if the animal allows.
Ensure clean dry bedding and milk only with washed hands and clean equipment.
Withhold milk from the food chain until a veterinarian advises it is safe.
Call a veterinarian promptly for antibiotics and pain management; severe cases can become systemic quickly.
Handle aborted materials and placenta only with gloves; bury or dispose as directed by a veterinarian.
Isolate aborted animals and separate their milk; do not consume raw milk from suspect animals.
Avoid assisting calving without protection when reproductive disease is suspected in the herd.
Record abortion dates and animal IDs for veterinary testing and herd screening.
Contact a veterinarian for blood testing and official control measures; do not treat alone with antibiotics without diagnosis.
